samples.question: What is FRTB and why does it matter for market risk?
samples.reference_answer: FRTB (Fundamental Review of the Trading Book) is a regulatory framework to improve market risk capital requirements after 2008. It increases risk sensitivity and model risk governance by introducing stricter requirements for risk factor eligibility, backtesting, and PnL attribution.

samples.answer:
1) TLDR
- Delta measures the sensitivity of a derivative's price to changes in the price of the underlying asset.
- Vanna is a second-order Greek that measures the sensitivity of Delta to changes in implied volatility.
- Charm measures the sensitivity of Delta to the passage of time, also known as delta decay.

- Delta is a sensitivity measure in derivatives risk.
- Vanna measures the sensitivity of Delta to changes in implied volatility.
- Charm measures the sensitivity of Delta to the passage of time (delta decay).

## 5. Counterparty risk and CVA

Counterparty risk is the risk that the counterparty defaults before final settlement.

CVA stands for Credit Valuation Adjustment.

A simplified intuition:

- CVA is an adjustment to the risk-free value.
- CVA increases when counterparty credit quality worsens.
- CVA depends on exposure profile over time.

In practice, CVA often interacts with collateral, netting sets, and wrong-way risk.

Key counterparty risk concepts:

- Netting set: a group of trades with a single counterparty that can be netted under a single master agreement (e.g., ISDA Master Agreement), reducing overall exposure by offsetting positive and negative mark-to-market values.
- CSA (Credit Support Annex): a legal document that supplements the ISDA Master Agreement, governing the terms for posting and receiving collateral between counterparties to mitigate credit risk.
- Wrong-way risk: occurs when exposure to a counterparty increases as the counterparty's credit quality deteriorates; for example, buying a put option from a bank on the bank's own stock.
- Right-way risk: the opposite of wrong-way risk; occurs when exposure to a counterparty decreases as the counterparty's credit quality deteriorates, reducing overall counterparty risk.

CVA was introduced as a new requirement for fair value accounting during the 2007/08 Global Financial Crisis. Market participants started incorporating credit valuation adjustment when calculating the value of over-the-counter derivative instruments.

The formula for calculating CVA is written with terms including maturity, discount factors, loss given default, default probability, and exposure over time.

# FRTB overview(ICMA)

Source: [https://www.icmagroup.org/market-practice-and-regulatory-policy/secondary-markets/secondary-markets-regulation/fundamental-review-of-the-trading-book-frtb/](https://www.icmagroup.org/market-practice-and-regulatory-policy/secondary-markets/secondary-markets-regulation/fundamental-review-of-the-trading-book-frtb/)

The Fundamental Review of the Trading Book (FRTB) is a comprehensive suite of capital rules developed by the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision (BCBS) as part of Basel III, intended to be applied to banks' wholesale trading activities. Finalised in January 2016 as the Minimum Capital Requirements for Market Risk, it aims to address a number of identified shortcomings in the existing Basel II.5 framework.

While FRTB was not intended to increase banks' capital costs beyond those imposed by Basel II.5, it is clear from both BCBS and industry analysis that banks will see significant increases in their cost of capital, in particular to support their trading activities.

In the EU, FRTB is being implemented as part of the Revised Capital Requirements Regulation (CRR II), and related Banking Package proposals.

## 4. FRTB overview

FRTB stands for Fundamental Review of the Trading Book.

The Fundamental Review of the Trading Book (FRTB) is a comprehensive suite of capital rules developed by the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision (BCBS) as part of Basel III, intended to be applied to banks' wholesale trading activities. Finalised in January 2016 as the Minimum Capital Requirements for Market Risk, it aims to address a number of identified shortcomings in the existing Basel II.5 framework.

While FRTB was not intended to increase banks' capital costs beyond those imposed by Basel II.5, it is clear from both BCBS and industry analysis that banks will see significant increases in their cost of capital, in particular to support their trading activities.

In the EU, FRTB is being implemented as part of the Revised Capital Requirements Regulation (CRR II), and related Banking Package proposals.

# CVA overview(CFI)

Source: [https://corporatefinanceinstitute.com/resources/derivatives/credit-valuation-adjustment-cva/](https://corporatefinanceinstitute.com/resources/derivatives/credit-valuation-adjustment-cva/)

Credit Valuation Adjustment (CVA) is the price that an investor would pay to hedge the counterparty credit risk of a derivative instrument. It reduces the mark to market value of an asset by the value of the CVA.

CVA was introduced as a new requirement for fair value accounting during the 2007/08 Global Financial Crisis. Market participants started incorporating credit valuation adjustment when calculating the value of over-the-counter derivative instruments.

The formula for calculating CVA is written with terms including maturity, discount factors, loss given default, default probability, and exposure over time.

1) TLDR
- The Basel Committee on Banking Supervision sets minimum capital requirements for market risk (January 2019, revised February 2019).
- It collaborates with the Board of the International Organization of Securities Commissions on margin requirements for non-centrally cleared derivatives (April 2020, July 2012).
- It addresses credit valuation adjustment risk through consultative documents (November 2019).

samples.answer:
1) TLDR
- FRTB was finalized in **January 2016** as the Minimum Capital Requirements for Market Risk.
- The standard was later revised in **January 2019 (rev. February 2019)** and integrated into the Basel Framework.

Citations: [source=corpus/regulatory_seed/pdf/en/bis_bcbs_d457.pdf chunk_id=bis_bcbs_d457.pdf:9b89f16f75e0] [source=corpus/regulatory_seed/pdf/en/bis_bcbs_d488.pdf chunk_id=bis_bcbs_d488.pdf:2dce0d7ae3fd] [source=corpus/acceptance/frtb_icma.md chunk_id=frtb_icma.md:27de361b6f41]

2) Key Facts
- The Fundamental Review of the Trading Book (FRTB) was finalized by the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision (BCBS) in **January 2016**.
- It was titled **Minimum Capital Requirements for Market Risk** and aimed to address shortcomings in Basel II.5.
- The standard was revised in **January 2019 (rev. February 2019)** and incorporated into the consolidated Basel Framework.

Citations: [source=corpus/regulatory_seed/pdf/en/bis_bcbs_d457.pdf chunk_id=bis_bcbs_d457.pdf:9b89f16f75e0] [source=corpus/regulatory_seed/pdf/en/bis_bcbs_d488.pdf chunk_id=bis_bcbs_d488.pdf:2dce0d7ae3fd] [source=corpus/acceptance/frtb_icma.md chunk_id=frtb_icma.md:27de361b6f41]

3) Why it matters
- FRTB was designed to improve capital rules for banks' wholesale trading activities under Basel III.
- It sought to correct deficiencies in the earlier Basel II.5 framework.

samples.answer:
1) TLDR
- Basel III is a set of standards finalized in December 2017 to address pre-crisis regulatory shortcomings and strengthen banking system resilience.
- One element of Basel III focuses on the Credit Valuation Adjustment (CVA) risk framework for banks engaging in derivatives or securities financing transactions.
- Implementation of Basel III was scheduled for 1 January 2022.

- Basel III standards were finalized in December 2017 as part of the Basel Committee’s response to the global financial crisis.
- The standards aim to correct pre-crisis regulatory weaknesses and ensure a resilient banking system supporting the real economy.
- A key component involves the CVA risk framework for banks conducting derivatives or securities financing transactions (SFTs).
- The Group of Central Bank Governors and Heads of Supervision endorsed the standards, expecting full implementation by 1 January 2022.

samples.question: What is the difference between trading book and banking book?
samples.reference_answer: Trading book contains assets held for trading, while banking book contains assets held to maturity. This distinction is important for FRTB.
ground_truth_contexts: Common concepts used in interviews and systems: Trading book vs banking book

qrels.text: Common concepts used in interviews and systems: Trading book vs banking book

samples.answer:
1) TLDR
- The **trading book** includes instruments subject to **market risk capital requirements**, while the **banking book** includes instruments subject to **credit risk capital requirements**.
- Instruments in the trading book must meet specific criteria outlined in [RBC25.2]–[RBC25.13]; all others default to the banking book.

Citations: [source=corpus/regulatory_seed/pdf/en/bis_bcbs_d457.pdf chunk_id=bis_bcbs_d457.pdf:2f8e50ce7774] [source=corpus/Background.md chunk_id=Background.md:9d9df405ddf4] [source=corpus/regulatory_seed/docx/en/isda_afme_frtb_position_paper.docx chunk_id=isda_afme_frtb_position_paper.docx:a844d523067b]

2) Key Facts
- The trading book consists of instruments (financial instruments, FX, commodities) meeting [RBC25.2]–[RBC25.13] criteria.
- The banking book includes all other instruments not qualifying for the trading book.
- Trading book instruments are subject to **market risk capital requirements**; banking book instruments face **credit risk capital requirements**.

Citations: [source=corpus/regulatory_seed/pdf/en/bis_bcbs_d457.pdf chunk_id=bis_bcbs_d457.pdf:2f8e50ce7774] [source=corpus/Background.md chunk_id=Background.md:9d9df405ddf4] [source=corpus/regulatory_seed/docx/en/isda_afme_frtb_position_paper.docx chunk_id=isda_afme_frtb_position_paper.docx:a844d523067b]

3) Why it matters
- The distinction determines whether **market risk** (trading book) or **credit risk** (banking book) capital requirements apply, impacting regulatory capital calculations.

The Fundamental Review of the Trading Book (FRTB) is a comprehensive suite of capital rules developed by the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision (BCBS) as part of Basel III, intended to be applied to banks' wholesale trading activities. Finalised in January 2016 as the Minimum Capital Requirements for Market Risk, it aims to address a number of identified shortcomings in the existing Basel II.5 framework.

While FRTB was not intended to increase banks' capital costs beyond those imposed by Basel II.5, it is clear from both BCBS and industry analysis that banks will see significant increases in their cost of capital, in particular to support their trading activities.

In the EU, FRTB is being implemented as part of the Revised Capital Requirements Regulation (CRR II), and related Banking Package proposals.

# CVA overview(CFI)

Source: [https://corporatefinanceinstitute.com/resources/derivatives/credit-valuation-adjustment-cva/](https://corporatefinanceinstitute.com/resources/derivatives/credit-valuation-adjustment-cva/)

Credit Valuation Adjustment (CVA) is the price that an investor would pay to hedge the counterparty credit risk of a derivative instrument. It reduces the mark to market value of an asset by the value of the CVA.

CVA was introduced as a new requirement for fair value accounting during the 2007/08 Global Financial Crisis. Market participants started incorporating credit valuation adjustment when calculating the value of over-the-counter derivative instruments.

The formula for calculating CVA is written with terms including maturity, discount factors, loss given default, default probability, and exposure over time.

## CRR 3 - Credit Valuation Adjustment (CVA) Risk


## February 2022


## Introduction

In July 2020, the BCBS published targeted revisions to the Credit Valuation Adjustment (CVA) framework, bringing final changes to the initial revised framework published in 2017, as part of the Basel III agreement. CVA refers to a measure of market risk incurred in the context of transactions or contracts involving counterparties (such as sovereign banks, other financial institutions, non-financial companies, etc.). In other words, as banks enter into derivatives contracts, they face the risk of incurring losses due to changes in the market value of those transactions and the deterioration of the creditworthiness of their counterparties.
Capital requirements for CVA risk are meant to require banks to hold aside capital to account for these losses. While the 2020 revisions attempted to solve some of the identified issues with the current CVA framework, further calibration is necessary to ensure that end-users, who typically use derivatives to hedge risk, are still able to access them at a reasonable cost. Particularly in the context of the recovery from the COVID-19 pandemic, it is crucial for banks to continue to support the real economy through the provision of these services and to not be constrained from doing so by an undue increase in the capital held against CVA risk. It is also important that the CVA framework is implemented in a coherent manner, and due consideration should be given to aligning the implementation timeline with the interlinked market risk standards.

Credit Valuation Adjustment (CVA) is the price that an investor would pay to hedge the counterparty credit risk of a derivative instrument. It reduces the mark to market value of an asset by the value of the CVA.

CVA was introduced as a new requirement for fair value accounting during the 2007/08 Global Financial Crisis. Market participants started incorporating credit valuation adjustment when calculating the value of over-the-counter derivative instruments.

The formula for calculating CVA is written with terms including maturity, discount factors, loss given default, default probability, and exposure over time.

## 3. Risk sensitivities (Greeks)

Greeks are sensitivities of a derivative value to small changes in risk factors.

Key Greeks:

- Delta: sensitivity to the underlying price level.
- Gamma: sensitivity of Delta to the underlying price.
- Vega: sensitivity to volatility.
- Theta: sensitivity of a derivative's value to the passage of time (also known as time decay).

Source: [https://gregorygundersen.com/blog/2023/10/08/greeks/](https://gregorygundersen.com/blog/2023/10/08/greeks/)

An option pricing model is a function that takes the price of the underlying asset, or spot price S, and other market inputs and outputs an option's fair value V.

An important way to understand an option-pricing model is to study the output price's sensitivity to the model's inputs. These partial derivatives are called the Greeks.

For example, the sensitivity of option price to spot is delta, written as dV/dS.

The most common choice for an option pricing model is the Black-Scholes equation, with inputs including spot price, strike price, time to expiry, volatility, and risk-free interest rate.

Source: [https://gregorygundersen.com/blog/2023/10/08/greeks/](https://gregorygundersen.com/blog/2023/10/08/greeks/)

An option pricing model is a function that takes the price of the underlying asset, or spot price S, and other market inputs and outputs an option's fair value V.

An important way to understand an option-pricing model is to study the output price's sensitivity to the model's inputs. These partial derivatives are called the Greeks.

For example, the sensitivity of option price to spot is delta, written as dV/dS.

The most common choice for an option pricing model is the Black-Scholes equation, with inputs including spot price, strike price, time to expiry, volatility, and risk-free interest rate.

- Credit spread risk (non-securitisation)
- Credit spread risk (securitisation: non-correlation trading portfolio)
- Credit spread risk (securitisation: correlation trading portfolio)
- FX risk
- Equity risk
- Commodity risk
- A **sensitivity** measures the change in an instrument's value due to a small change in one of its underlying risk factors (e.g., delta and vega risks).

samples.reference_answer: Counterparty credit risk is the risk that a counterparty will default on its obligations, which is addressed by CVA.

samples.answer:
1) TLDR
- Counterparty credit risk is the risk that the counterparty defaults before final settlement.
- CVA (Credit Valuation Adjustment) adjusts the risk-free value based on counterparty credit quality.
- Netting sets and collateral agreements (e.g., CSA) mitigate counterparty risk.

Citations: [source=corpus/Background.md chunk_id=Background.md:02a6daa31fa9] [source=corpus/Background.md chunk_id=Background.md:bfd07d611b41] [source=corpus/Background.md chunk_id=Background.md:bbdac6808ba2]

2) Key Facts
- Counterparty risk arises if the counterparty defaults before final settlement.
- CVA is an adjustment to the risk-free value, increasing as counterparty credit quality worsens.
- Netting sets reduce exposure by offsetting positive and negative mark-to-market values under a master agreement (e.g., ISDA).
- A CSA governs collateral terms to mitigate credit risk.
- Wrong-way risk occurs when exposure rises as counterparty credit quality declines (e.g., buying a put option on a bank's stock from that bank).

3) Why it matters
- CVA reflects the cost of counterparty risk in pricing derivatives.
- Mitigation tools (netting, collateral) are critical for managing exposure.

## 5. Counterparty risk and CVA

Counterparty risk is the risk that the counterparty defaults before final settlement.

CVA stands for Credit Valuation Adjustment.

A simplified intuition:

- CVA is an adjustment to the risk-free value.
- CVA increases when counterparty credit quality worsens.
- CVA depends on exposure profile over time.

In practice, CVA often interacts with collateral, netting sets, and wrong-way risk.

Key counterparty risk concepts:

- Netting set: a group of trades with a single counterparty that can be netted under a single master agreement (e.g., ISDA Master Agreement), reducing overall exposure by offsetting positive and negative mark-to-market values.

qrels.text: A CSA is a legal document that governs collateral arrangements between counterparties to mitigate counterparty risk.

samples.answer:
1) TLDR
- A CSA (Credit Support Annex) is a legal document supplementing the ISDA Master Agreement that governs collateral terms to mitigate credit risk.
- It defines rules for posting and receiving collateral between counterparties.

## 5. Counterparty risk and CVA

Counterparty risk is the risk that the counterparty defaults before final settlement.

CVA stands for Credit Valuation Adjustment.

A simplified intuition:

- CVA is an adjustment to the risk-free value.
- CVA increases when counterparty credit quality worsens.
- CVA depends on exposure profile over time.

In practice, CVA often interacts with collateral, netting sets, and wrong-way risk.

Key counterparty risk concepts:

- Netting set: a group of trades with a single counterparty that can be netted under a single master agreement (e.g., ISDA Master Agreement), reducing overall exposure by offsetting positive and negative mark-to-market values.
- CSA (Credit Support Annex): a legal document that supplements the ISDA Master Agreement, governing the terms for posting and receiving collateral between counterparties to mitigate credit risk.
- Wrong-way risk: occurs when exposure to a counterparty increases as the counterparty's credit quality deteriorates; for example, buying a put option from a bank on the bank's own stock.
- Right-way risk: the opposite of wrong-way risk; occurs when exposure to a counterparty decreases as the counterparty's credit quality deteriorates, reducing overall counterparty risk.

samples.question: What is variation margin?
samples.reference_answer: Variation margin is collateral exchanged daily to mark-to-market current exposure.

qrels.text: Variation margin is collateral exchanged daily to mark-to-market current exposure.

samples.answer:
1) TLDR
- Variation margin is the mandatory exchange of funds representing the settlement of running profit/loss of a derivative, with no net liquidity costs.
- It is part of margin requirements for non-centrally cleared derivatives, alongside initial margin.

Citations: [source=corpus/regulatory_seed/pdf/en/iosco_iq_margin_2020.pdf chunk_id=iosco_iq_margin_2020.pdf:0945220c1016] [source=corpus/regulatory_seed/pdf/en/iosco_iq_margin_2020.pdf chunk_id=iosco_iq_margin_2020.pdf:bc11b4e6978d] [source=corpus/regulatory_seed/pdf/en/iosco_iq_margin_2013_consultation.pdf chunk_id=iosco_iq_margin_2013_consultation.pdf:6d8e69f2465f]

2) Key Facts
- Variation margin is exchanged regularly and timely between parties to non-centrally cleared derivatives.
- It reflects the current exposure of a derivative portfolio, unlike initial margin, which reflects potential future exposure.
- The BCBS and IOSCO endorse variation margin as part of universal two-way margin requirements.

Citations: [source=corpus/regulatory_seed/pdf/en/iosco_iq_margin_2020.pdf chunk_id=iosco_iq_margin_2020.pdf:bc11b4e6978d] [source=corpus/regulatory_seed/pdf/en/iosco_iq_margin_2020.pdf chunk_id=iosco_iq_margin_2020.pdf:0945220c1016] [source=corpus/regulatory_seed/pdf/en/iosco_iq_margin_2013_consultation.pdf chunk_id=iosco_iq_margin_2013_consultation.pdf:6d8e69f2465f]

3) Why it matters
- Variation margin ensures counterparty risk exposures are covered in non-centrally cleared derivatives.
- Its calculation must be consistent across entities to maintain fairness and risk coverage.

supported_sentences: - Variation margin is the mandatory exchange of funds representing the settlement of running profit/loss of a derivative, with no net liquidity costs
- It is part of margin requirements for non-centrally cleared derivatives, alongside initial margin
- Variation margin is exchanged regularly and timely between parties to non-centrally cleared derivatives
- It reflects the current exposure of a derivative portfolio, unlike initial margin, which reflects potential future exposure
- The BCBS and IOSCO endorse variation margin as part of universal two-way margin requirements

samples.question: What is value at risk (VaR)?
samples.reference_answer: VaR is a measure of potential loss over a given horizon at a given confidence level.

qrels.text: VaR is a measure of potential loss over a given horizon at a given confidence level.

samples.answer:
1) TLDR
- Value at risk (VaR) measures the worst expected loss on a portfolio from market movements over a given time horizon and confidence level.
- VaR is used alongside expected shortfall (ES) in regulatory risk measure reports for trading desks.

Citations: [source=corpus/regulatory_seed/pdf/en/bis_bcbs_d457.pdf chunk_id=bis_bcbs_d457.pdf:76cbf35975bf] [source=corpus/regulatory_seed/pdf/en/bis_bcbs_d457.pdf chunk_id=bis_bcbs_d457.pdf:e62b6154a564] [source=corpus/regulatory_seed/pdf/en/cftc_2020_27736_margin_uncleared_swaps.pdf chunk_id=cftc_2020_27736_margin_uncleared_swaps.pdf:8561f1e08677]

2) Key Facts
- VaR is defined as "a measure of the worst expected loss on a portfolio of instruments resulting from market movements over a given time horizon and a pre-defined confidence level."
- Banks must report trading desk VaR/ES as part of internal and regulatory risk measure reports.

Citations: [source=corpus/regulatory_seed/pdf/en/bis_bcbs_d457.pdf chunk_id=bis_bcbs_d457.pdf:76cbf35975bf] [source=corpus/regulatory_seed/pdf/en/bis_bcbs_d457.pdf chunk_id=bis_bcbs_d457.pdf:e62b6154a564] [source=corpus/regulatory_seed/pdf/en/cftc_2020_27736_margin_uncleared_swaps.pdf chunk_id=cftc_2020_27736_margin_uncleared_swaps.pdf:8561f1e08677]

3) Why it matters
- VaR is part of the market risk framework, used alongside stress scenarios and other metrics to assess capital requirements and trading desk exposures.
